paras: The flogging of Charles Johnson was the whipping of a Black man by a posse in Monroe County, Mississippi, in March 1903, after he was accused of stealing the horse of Hutch Walton, the farmer who had paid him out of jail. Johnson was captured near Amory and returned to the county jail. The flogging became known through a short state-news paragraph headed "Flogged the Negro" that ran in several Mississippi weeklies.

Johnson had been held in the Monroe County jail for petit larceny, serving either a term or a fine, according to different reports. Walton, of the Hamilton neighborhood, paid him out and took him to his farm "to work out the amount of the sentence," as the Aberdeen weekly put it.

Shortly afterward Johnson was accused of taking Walton's saddle horse and leaving; the Aberdeen paper placed this on "the following Saturday night," while the state-news paragraph said "the next night." After a pursuit, he was captured on Sunday morning riding the horse toward his old home at Amory. According to the state-news paragraph, the capture was made by "a posse headed by Walton," and Johnson "was treated to a flogging and jailed."
Johnson was returned to the county jail, but no report of a trial on the horse charge or of any action against the men who whipped him appears in the coverage.

The first report came from the Aberdeen weekly, published in the county, on March 27, which said Johnson "repaid Mr. Walton's kindness" by stealing the horse and made no mention of a flogging. A week later a brief item headed "Flogged the Negro" appeared in the Hernando Times-Promoter on April 3 among other state news. The same paragraph and headline ran the next day in the Woodville Republican, the Macon beacon and the Grenada sentinel.
Both versions presented the theft as fact and reported the whipping in a matter-of-fact phrase, without comment on its legality. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The flogging rests on the state-news paragraph alone, since the earlier local account describes only the pursuit, capture and return to jail. The two versions also differ on timing, and the Aberdeen weekly, as the local and earlier report, gives the more specific account of the Saturday-night departure and Sunday-morning capture.

reader.title: Flogging of Charles Johnson
bases: A posse headed by the man who had paid Johnson out of jail captured and flogged him before returning him to jail, with no organized band or attempt to kill reported (A1, A3).

The flogging rests on one state-news paragraph (A3, reprinted A4-A6); the independent local report (A1) corroborates the payout, the horse accusation, the pursuit, capture and jailing but does not mention a flogging.

accounts.label: Aberdeen local report
accounts.gist: Johnson repaid Walton's 'kindness' by taking his saddle horse on Saturday night; after pursuit he was captured Sunday morning riding toward Amory and returned to jail, with no flogging mentioned.

accounts.label: State-news paragraph
accounts.gist: Johnson took Walton's horse the night after being paid out, was captured near Amory by a posse headed by Walton, 'treated to a flogging and jailed.'

framing.detail: The Aberdeen weekly treated the theft as fact and the capture as the due reward of ingratitude, saying Johnson 'repaid Mr. Walton's kindness' by stealing the horse.
The state-news paragraph headed 'Flogged the Negro' reported the flogging flatly, as 'treated to a flogging', without comment.
The Woodville Republican, Macon beacon and Grenada sentinel ran the same paragraph and headline on 1903-04-04.
